title: Nirvana Day
hook: February 15 in East Asia: the Buddha's passing remembered

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rohatsu, the night of awakening, and your line, the morning star. Did you catch a star, or the first light, before the day got loud? Today, the other end of the same life. Day six hundred ninety-two.

In a temple in Japan in mid-February, a huge painted scroll is unrolled and hung. In the middle, a man lies on his right side between trees, head resting on his hand. Around him, crowds are weeping: monks, kings, gods. And animals. An elephant on its back. A tiger. Birds, a snake, a crowd of creatures. It's called a nehan-zu, a picture of nirvana. And it isn't a picture of awakening. It's a picture of a death. Today is Nirvana Day.
screen: `A SCROLL UNROLLED IN FEBRUARY.` → `THE ANIMALS WEEPING.` → `A PICTURE OF A DEATH.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Buddhists use the word nirvana for two things. One is the awakening itself, the fire of craving going out, which we kept yesterday. The other is what happens when an awakened one dies: the final nirvana, parinirvana in Sanskrit, parinibbana in Pali. Nothing is left to be reborn. Nirvana Day remembers that second one. In Japan it's usually kept on February 15; other Mahayana communities keep it then too, or on February 8, or by the lunar calendar. In Theravada lands, as we heard on Vesak, the passing is kept on the same full moon as the birth and the awakening. Same event, different calendars, and nobody is wrong about it. Now the story, from the Book of the Great Decease. The Buddha is eighty. He's ill. He walks to Kusinara, a small town, and lies down between two sal trees. The text says the trees burst into flower out of season and dropped blossoms on him. His cousin Ananda goes off and weeps against a doorpost. The Buddha calls him back, and reminds him: hadn't he always taught that everything dear must change and part? Then he asks the monks three times if anyone has a last doubt. Nobody speaks. And then come his last words. In Rhys Davids's translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Notice what he does with his own death. He doesn't hide it. He uses it as the final lesson. Things put together come apart, including a Buddha. So keep going, carefully. On Nirvana Day, temples chant, read the story, sit. Some temples make little dumplings or rice cakes. The point isn't grief. It's looking straight at an ending, with company.
screen: `TWO MEANINGS OF NIRVANA.` · `A PASSING ON TWO CALENDARS.` · `BETWEEN THE SAL TREES.` · `THE LAST WORDS AS A LESSON.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one ending. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then let one ending come to mind. Not the hardest one you know. Maybe a school, a house, a friendship that drifted, a pet, a season of life. Look at it the way the scroll looks at the Buddha: plainly, with company around. What was it? What did it give you? If grief comes, let it sit with you too. Ananda wept. At the end, come back to this breath, which is also ending, and the next one, which is beginning. The bell holds the time.
Nirvana Day. February 15 in East Asian Buddhism, remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana between the sal trees. Today's word.
Your line: all things end. Today, when something small finishes, a meal, a song, a conversation, notice it end, and let it go without rushing to the next thing. Day six hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: In Japan and many Mahayana communities, temples mark Nirvana Day (Nehan-e) around February 15 by hanging a painting of the Buddha's passing, chanting, and reading from the account of his last days; Theravada Buddhists remember the passing on Vesak.

fork.setup: you are the Buddha, dying. your closest friend is sobbing outside. what do you do?
options: call him back and remind him all dear things change.
fork.reveal: he calls Ananda back, comforts him, praises his years of care, and reminds him that whatever is dear must change and part.

original.note: Sanskrit parinirvana: complete going-out, the final nirvana at an awakened one's death; Pali parinibbana.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirvana day is the day the Buddha reached nirvana.
what it means: it marks his parinirvana, the final passing at Kusinara, not the awakening.
what a scholar hears: the account is the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16, which follows his last journey town by town.
recall: things to remember, that make dear

notes: Quotation from Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas (SBE vol. 11, 1881), Book of the Great Decease VI.10; please confirm exact wording and punctuation.

Confirm February 15 for Nehan-e in Japan and the claim that many East Asian and Western Mahayana communities keep it then (some keep it on February 8 or by the lunar calendar). Reviewer softened the teach line to 'usually kept on February 15' in Japan, with February 8 and lunar dates named for other communities.
Nehan-zu details (animals mourning around the Buddha, an elephant on its back) are typical of the paintings; please confirm.
